title: Growing oca
subtitle: A South American tuber with a tangy, lemony flavour that stores well over winter.
excerpt: Oca is a perennial South American root crop grown as an annual in the UK. Plant the small tubers in spring and harvest in November after the first frost has sweetened the crop. The flavour is lemony and slightly sharp when freshly dug, and sweetens over a week or two of storage.
sourceNotes: Cultivation notes from Martin Crawford, Creating a Forest Garden (2010) and Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org). Day-length sensitivity note from New World root crop research. UK growing experience documented in heritage vegetable grower sources.

glossaryTerms.definition: A root crop that only forms tubers once day length falls below a critical threshold, usually in autumn. Oca and some yam varieties are short-day crops. In the UK, this means tubers do not begin to form until October, so the growing season must run as late as possible before the first hard frost.

content.text: from the Andes. In the UK, the plants make no tubers until October, when shortening days trigger tuber formation. For this reason, the season must run as long as possible: plant late (May) and harvest after the first frost (November). Early frosts cut the season short and reduce yields significantly.

Plant tubers in May, 10 cm deep, 30 to 45 cm apart. Start in pots if you want an earlier start: pot up in April under glass and plant out after frosts have passed in late May. The plants grow to about 30 to 45 cm in height and spread low across the ground.

Earth up the stems in midsummer, as with potatoes. This encourages more tubers to form along the buried stems. The plants produce small yellow flowers in late summer but they are not important for yield. Keep the bed weeded until the plants cover the ground.

Do not dig until the foliage has been frosted. The tubers can be left in the ground for two to three weeks after frost, as long as the ground does not freeze hard. Dig carefully: the tubers are clustered near the surface and are easily damaged.
Store tubers in a cool, dry, dark place. The flavour improves over two to three weeks in storage as the oxalic acid breaks down and the starch converts to sugar. Eat within two months.

attrs.title: Frost protection for a longer season
attrs.body: If an early October frost threatens before the tubers have bulked up, cover the plants with fleece overnight. Fleece gives two to three degrees of frost protection. Extending the season by even two weeks can double the yield, since tubers are still actively forming in October. Remove the fleece during the day to allow continued growth.
